overview.body:
**Ninigi** ​(*ninigi*) — ‌Rice, Descendant ‌of ​Amaterasu · ​The ​august rice ​spirit — ​belongs ‌to the ​Japanese ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Rice, ‌Descendant ​of Amaterasu". ​The ​name means ​"The august ​rice ‌spirit"[^1].

**Ninigi** ​is ‌the grandson ​of Amaterasu, ‌sent ​from heaven ‌to ​rule the ‌terrestrial world ​and ​establish the ‌imperial line. ‌He ‌descended to ​Takachiho ​in Kyūshū ‌bearing the ​Three ​Sacred Regalia ‌— ​the mirror, ​the sword, ‌and ​the jewel ‌— and ​his ​great-grandson became ​Emperor ​Jimmu, the ‌legendary first ‌emperor ​of Japan.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ​restores the ​name as ‌**Ninigi** ‌and serves ‌its temple ‌at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/ninigi/). ‌The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a ‌description computed ​from ​the displayed ​form itself. ‌The ​plain ASCII ​form ​*ninigi* survives ‌as a ​modern ‌convenience imposed ​by the ‌early ​domain-name system; ‌the ‌restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Kojiki, Book I (descent, Ōkuninushi's withdrawal, the ordeal of fire).
Nihon Shoki, Books I–III (parallel and variant accounts).
Philippi, Kojiki (translation).

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested in ​Japanese ​characters ​as ​**邇邇芸命**. ​Etymologically it ‌means ​"The ​august ‌rice ​spirit"[^1].

The ‌ASCII ​form ‌*ninigi* ​survives ​only because ​the ​early ​domain-name ‌system ​could not ‌carry ​diacritics; ‌it ​is ‌a technological ​compromise, ‌not ​an ​ancient ‌spelling. ‌The Unicode ‌restoration ​**Ninigi** ​recovers ‌the ​full diacritic ​detail ‌of ​the ​scholarly ‌transliteration directly ​in ‌the ​address ​bar. ​The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ‌form ‌— ​a ‌description computed ​from ​the ‌displayed ‌form ‌itself.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ​**n** ​→ ​**N** — ‌Same, ​capitalized
- ​**i** ​→ ‌**i** — ​Same
- ​**n** ​→ ‌**n** ​— Same
- ‌**i** ​→ ‌**i** ​— ‌Same
- **g** ‌→ ​**g** ​— ​Same
- ​**i** → ‌**i** ‌— ​Same

sources.citation: Kojiki, Book I (descent, Ōkuninushi's withdrawal, the ordeal of fire).

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name ​is **/ni.ni.ɡi/** ​— ​Modern Standard ​Japanese (Hepburn).[^1]

​Phoneme ‌by phoneme:

- ​**Ni-** ​— Alveolar ‌nasal [n] ​plus ‌close front ​[i]
- **-ni-** ‌— ​Alveolar nasal ​[n] ​plus close ​front [i]
- ​**-gi** ‌— Voiced ​velar ‌stop [ɡ] ​plus close ‌front ​[i]; from ‌邇邇芸, ​whose final ‌character associates ​him ​with rice ‌and skill

‌For ‌the modern ​speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'NEE-nee-gee' ​— light, ‌even ​syllables; the ​'g' is ‌hard.

​Kindred and ‌historical forms ​of ​the name:

- ​**Japanese** ​— 邇邇芸命 ‌(Ninigi-no-mikoto), 'The ‌August ​Grandchild of ‌the ​Rice' (Kojiki, ​Book I)
- ‌**Grandmother** ‌— Amaterasu, ‌the sun ‌goddess ​who sent ‌him ​down (Kojiki, ​Book I)
- ​**Descendant** ‌— Great-grandfather ​of ​Emperor Jimmu ​(Nihon Shoki, ‌Books ​I–III)

Ninigi ​keeps ​its restoration ‌plain: plain ​Hepburn ‌with no ​distinctive feature ‌for ​the ASCII ‌form ‌to lose. ​He is ​the ​heavenly grandson ​sent ‌to rule ‌the terrestrial ​world.

sources.citation: Kojiki, Book I (descent, Ōkuninushi's withdrawal, the ordeal of fire).

domains.body:
**Ninigi** ​is the ‌grandson ‌of Amaterasu, ​sent ​from heaven ​to ​rule the ​terrestrial world ‌and ​establish the ​imperial ‌line. He ​descended ‌to Takachiho ​in ‌Kyūshū bearing ​the ​Three Sacred ​Regalia ​— the ​mirror, ‌the sword, ​and the ‌jewel ​— and ‌his ​great-grandson became ‌Emperor ​Jimmu, the ‌legendary ​first emperor ​of ‌Japan.[^1]

### Bearer ‌of ‌the Regalia

​He ​carried the ‌mirror Yata, ​the ​sword Kusanagi, ‌and ​the jewel ​Yasakani ‌from heaven ​to ‌earth — ​the ​warrant of ​every ​later throne.

### ‌Heavenly Descent

‌Amaterasu ​sent him ‌to ​rule the ​land ‌of reed ‌plains ‌— the ‌tenson ​kōrin, the ‌founding ​descent of ​Japanese ​sovereignty.

### Imperial ‌Ancestor

His ​line ​produced Hoori, ​Ugayafukiaezu, ‌and Jimmu ​— ​four generations ​from ‌heaven to ​Kashihara.

### ‌Rice Spirit

​His ‌name's final ​character, ‌芸, ties ‌him to ​rice ​and skill ​— ​agricultural sovereignty ‌in ‌a single ​syllable.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki, Books I–III (parallel and variant accounts).
Kojiki, Book I (descent, Ōkuninushi's withdrawal, the ordeal of fire).

mythology.body:
Ninigi's mythology is the bridge ​between the heavenly realm of Amaterasu and the ‌earthly rule of the emperors: four scenes — the ‌descent, the negotiated surrender of the land, the ​ordeal by fire that proved his wife's fidelity, and ​the genealogy that produced Jimmu — suffice to ​carry three regalia and a nation from the Floating ​Bridge of Heaven to Kashihara.[^1]

### The Descent from ​Heaven (Kojiki I)

When Amaterasu resolved that the ‌land of reed plains should be governed from heaven, ​she chose not her son but her grandson. ​She gave Ninigi the Three Sacred Regalia — the ‌mirror Yata, the sword Kusanagi that Susanoo had ​won from the eight-forked serpent, and the curved jewel ‌Yasakani — and sent him down, escorted by ​the deities Ame-no-koyane and Futodama, from the Floating Bridge ‌of Heaven to Takachiho in Kyūshū. The *Kojiki* ​(Book I) frames the descent as a transfer of ​title: heaven holds sovereignty, and the earth must ​receive it. One detail sharpens the stakes. As Ninigi ​left, Amaterasu told him the mirror was to ​be worshipped as her own spirit — the warrant ‌of his rule was simultaneously her presence. A ​thousand generations of imperial ideology condensed into a ‌single instruction: the emperor rules because he carries what ​Ninigi carried. The myth means that legitimacy, in ‌the Japanese telling, is a thing handed down, not ​taken.[^2]

### Ōkuninushi's Withdrawal (Kojiki I)

The earth, however, ‌was occupied. Its master, the great kami Ōkuninushi, had ​built and governed the land — some say ‌he had won it by ordeal and war — ​and heaven's envoy could not simply take it. ​The *Kojiki* (Book I) tells how Ninigi pressed the ‌matter through negotiation rather than battle, with pressure ‌from the celestial host. Ōkuninushi consulted his sons; his ‌wise son Kotoshironushi, recognising heaven's claim, withdrew of ​his own accord and is still honored at Mount ​Miwa. His father then set his price: a ‌great sanctuary built for him at Kizuki in ​Izumo — the origin of the shrine now called ​Izumo Ōyashiro — and the keeping of the ‌land's hidden, numinous affairs. In one stroke the myth ​explains two of Japan's greatest shrines and establishes ​a template of Japanese statecraft: conquest by diplomacy, and ‌the defeated party honored, not erased. The *Nihon ​Shoki* gives variant versions, but the pattern holds. The ‌myth's deepest meaning may be that sovereignty is ​best taken by leaving the former holder something greater ​than his loss.

### The Ordeal of Fire (Kojiki ​I)

Standing one day at Cape Kasasa, Ninigi saw ​a woman more beautiful than any other and ‌asked her name. She was Konohanasakuya-hime, daughter of ‌the mountain-god Ōyamatsumi; she consented, and that same night ​conceived. Ninigi doubted her when the pregnancy showed ‌at once — whose child could be born in ​a day? The princess answered with fire. She ​entered a parturition hut, sealed it, and set it ‌alight, vowing that if the children were truly ‌Ninigi's they would be unharmed. In the midst of ‌the flames she delivered three sons: Hoderi, the ‌luck of the sea; Hoori, the luck of the ​mountains; and Hosuseri. Mother and infants survived, and ‌Ninigi's suspicion was answered with living proof. The episode ​is one of the most vivid ordeal-births in ​world mythology, and it quietly elevates the bride: it ​is her fidelity, tested by fire, that founds ‌the dynasty. The myth means that legitimacy flows ​not from the doubting husband but through the mother ​whose truth outlasts the flames.

### From Ninigi to ​Jimmu (Nihon Shoki)

The *Nihon Shoki* (Books I–III) completes ‌the genealogy. Hoori, the mountain-lucky son, married Toyotama-hime, ​daughter of the sea-god, and their son Ugayafukiaezu wed ​his aunt Tamayori-hime; of that union was born ​Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko, who marched east from Hyūga, fought through the ‌Kumaso, and acceded at Kashihara — Emperor Jimmu, ​the legendary first emperor. Ninigi is thus Jimmu's great-grandfather, ‌and every imperial genealogy in Japanese history has ​run through him. The same chapters preserve the succession ‌stories the official line passed over: in one ​*Nihon Shoki* variant, Ninigi's elder brother Ame-no-hohi was sent ‌to the earth first and never returned, and ‌Ninigi's descent was the second attempt. The sources ​are candid that more than one heir was considered. ​The myth's function is transparent and, for over ​a millennium, was effectively constitutional: it makes the emperor ​a descendant of Amaterasu in the fourth generation. ‌It means that the state located its origin not ‌in a conquest but in a birth — ​a genealogy, not a battlefield.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki, Books I–III (parallel and variant accounts).
Philippi, Kojiki (translation).

syncretism.body:
Ninigi ​was never ‌a popularly ‌worshipped god, ​and that ​absence is ​itself revealing. ​His role ​was absorbed ‌into two ​institutions: the ​imperial ‌house, which ​descends from ‌him, and ​State Shinto, ‌which taught ​his descent ​as the ​founding act ​of the ​Japanese nation. ‌In ​the Meiji ‌period the ​*tenson kōrin* ‌became civic ​doctrine, and ‌Jimmu's traditional ​accession date ‌anchored the ​national holiday ​Kigensetsu. After ‌1945 ‌the emperor's ‌divinity was ​renounced, and ​Ninigi settled ‌back into ​mythology — ​taught in ‌schools, visited ​at Takachiho, ​but rarely ‌prayed ​to. Buddhism, ‌meanwhile, largely ​ignored him: ​he is ​one of ​the few ‌major kami ‌without a ​Buddhist avatar ‌(*honji*). His ​syncretic ​afterlife is ‌thus mostly ‌political memory ‌— the ‌story a ​state told ‌about where ​its authority ​came from.[^1]

​Kindred figures ‌in ​the PuniCodex ​cross-tradition index ​include [[amaterasu|Amaterasu]] ‌(solar grandmother ​and divine ​grandson), [[anahita|Anāhitā]] ​(earth / ‌mother / ​fertility), [[audhumla|Auðhumla]] ‌(earth / ​mother ‌/ fertility), ​[[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]] (earth ‌/ mother ‌/ fertility), ​[[bastet|Bꜣstt]] (earth ​/ mother ​/ fertility), ​and [[cernunnos|Cernunnos]] ‌(earth / ‌mother / ​fertility).

sources.citation: Kojiki, Book I (descent, Ōkuninushi's withdrawal, the ordeal of fire).

cultural-legacy.body: Ninigi's ​legacy ‌is carried ‌by ​objects ​and places ​rather ​than ​temples. The ‌Three ​Sacred ​Regalia he ‌bore ​— ‌mirror, sword, ​jewel ‌— ​remain the ​symbols ​of ​imperial legitimacy, ​presented ‌at ​each ‌accession though ​never ‌publicly ​displayed. Takachiho ‌in ​Miyazaki ‌Prefecture, his ​traditional ​landing ‌place, draws ‌pilgrims ‌and ​visitors to ​the ‌Ama-no-Iwato ​shrine and ​the ‌gorge ​of the ​descent; ‌Kashihara ​Jingū ‌in Nara ​marks ​where ​his great-grandson ​Jimmu ‌is ‌said to ​have ‌acceded. ​The *Kojiki* ​(712) ‌and ‌*Nihon Shoki* ‌(720) ‌preserve ​his story ‌as ​the ​hinge between ​gods ‌and ​emperors. ​In a ​Japan ‌that ​no longer ​claims ​divine ‌descent, Ninigi ​endures ‌as ​the mythological ‌explanation ​of ‌why the ‌islands ​were ​long thought ​to ​belong ‌to one ‌unbroken ​line.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, Book I (descent, Ōkuninushi's withdrawal, the ordeal of fire).

archaeology.body: No ​artifact can ‌be ‌tied to ​Ninigi himself, ​but ​the geography ​of ​his myth ‌is mapped ​in ​standing shrines. ‌Takachiho ​in Miyazaki ‌Prefecture ​keeps the ‌sites of ​the ​descent — ​the ​Ama-no-Iwato ('Cave ​of ‌Heaven') shrine ​and the ‌sheer ​gorge where, ‌by ​tradition, he ‌first set ​foot ‌on earth. ​Izumo ​Ōyashiro in ‌Shimane, ‌rebuilt in ‌its monumental ​ancient ​form, marks ‌the ​sanctuary Ōkuninushi ​demanded ‌as the ​price of ​withdrawing; ‌excavations in ​2000 ‌uncovered pillar ​bases suggesting ​an ​ancient structure ​of ‌unprecedented height. ‌Kashihara ​Jingū in ‌Nara stands ​at ​the foot ‌of ‌Unebi-yama, the ‌traditional ‌accession site ​of Jimmu, ‌Ninigi's ​great-grandson. The ​regalia ​he carried ‌are kept ​at ​Ise (the ​mirror), ‌Atsuta (the ​sword), ​and the ​palace (the ‌jewel) ​— none ‌ever ​displayed or ‌archaeologically ​examined. Ninigi's ‌material record ‌is ​thus a ​landscape ​of shrines ​rather than ‌a ‌museum of ​objects.[^1]

meditation.body:
Ninigi ​is the ‌moment when ‌heaven ​touches earth. ​He carries ​divine authority ​not ​as force ‌but as ​gift ​— the ‌mirror that ​sees ‌truly, the ​sword that ‌cuts ​cleanly, the ​jewel that ​holds abundance ​— ​and his ‌story asks ​what ‌it means ​to receive ‌power ​and pass ‌it on. ​He ‌is, notably, ​a mediocre ​protagonist: he ‌doubts ‌his wife, ‌wins no ​battles, ​performs no ‌miracles. The ​tradition ​seems uninterested ‌in his ​character ​because his ‌function is ​transmission, not ‌heroism. ​He is ​a conduit, ​and ​the myth ‌honors the ‌conduit ​more than ‌the current.

​That ​is a ‌quietly radical ‌theology of ‌legitimacy. ‌Authority is ​not earned ‌in ​the descent ​but entrusted ​before ‌it, and ​its proof ​is ​not the ‌bearer's virtue ​but the ​unbroken ​line that ‌follows him. ​Every ‌institution that ​inherits rather ‌than ​conquers its ‌mandate — ‌every ​regency, every ​relay, every ​succession — ​retells ‌Ninigi's descent ‌without knowing ​it.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, Book I (descent, Ōkuninushi's withdrawal, the ordeal of fire).

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
Japan's two earliest chronicles, the Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE), record Ninigi in mythic narratives of cosmogony and imperial descent. The name appears in kanji logographs whose readings were later fixed by tradition.

The restoration Ninigi preserves the romanized scholarly form derived from those classical sources.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, Book I (descent, Ōkuninushi's withdrawal, the ordeal of fire).

shinto-sources.body:
Shinto ritual texts, shrine records, and norito prayers preserve the cultic identity of Ninigi. The kami is honored at shrines associated with rice, and festival calendars perpetuate the name.

The Unicode form Ninigi gives that ongoing tradition a precise digital address.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, Book I (descent, Ōkuninushi's withdrawal, the ordeal of fire).

buddhist-japanese.body:
Japanese Buddhist literature and art sometimes assimilate Ninigi into Buddhist cosmology, mapping kami onto dharmic protectors and bodhisattvas. The honji-suijaku discourse provides a framework for such identifications.

The restored name Ninigi appears in both Shinto and Buddhist contexts in the PuniCodex archive.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, Book I (descent, Ōkuninushi's withdrawal, the ordeal of fire).
